title: MOS capacitor structure and gate contact potential

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A **MOS capacitor** is a stack of gate (metal or heavily doped n+ polysilicon), a thin silicon dioxide insulator, and the silicon body, which here is p-type. It is a parallel-plate capacitor in which one plate is a semiconductor, so the "plate" can bend, deplete and invert.

Even with 0 V applied between gate and body, the gate and body sit at different potentials because they are different materials: this is the **contact potential**. Measured from intrinsic silicon, an n+ poly gate sits near \(+0.55\ \mathrm{V}\) (its Fermi level is near the conduction band) and the p body sits at \(\varphi_p < 0\). The difference must be dropped across the oxide and the silicon surface, so the bands are already bent at zero bias.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ C_{ox} = \frac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{t_{ox}}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ox} = 3.9\varepsilon_0 = 3.45\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{F/cm} \]
\[ \varphi_p = -V_{th}\ln\frac{N_A}{n_i}, \qquad \varphi_{n^+} \approx +0.55\ \mathrm{V} \]
Built-in gate-to-body potential: \(\varphi_{n^+} - \varphi_p\).
Unit help: \(1\ \mathrm{F/cm^2} = 10^{7}\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
An n+ poly gate on p-type silicon with \(N_A = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and \(t_{ox} = 4\ \mathrm{nm}\):
\[ \varphi_p = -0.026\ln10^{5} \approx -0.30\ \mathrm{V} \]
\[ \varphi_{n^+} - \varphi_p \approx 0.55 + 0.30 = 0.85\ \mathrm{V} \]
\[ C_{ox} = \frac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{t_{ox}} = \frac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{4\ \mathrm{nm}} \approx 8.6\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2} \]

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(\varepsilon_{si}\) (11.7) instead of \(\varepsilon_{ox}\) (3.9) for the oxide.
- Forgetting nm-to-cm conversion: \(1\ \mathrm{nm} = 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm}\).
- Giving the p body a positive potential.
- Assuming zero applied voltage means flat bands.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: From here you will bias the gate and watch the surface move through accumulation, depletion and inversion, then derive the threshold voltage that sets when a MOSFET turns on.
